data.title: Tinea corporis / cruris / faciei — viva
data.summary: Fungal infections · 17 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tinea corporis / cruris / faciei** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. Define dermatophytosis. Classify fungal infections (common PYQ).**
- Dermatophytosis: infection of keratinised tissues (stratum corneum, hair, nails) by dermatophytes — keratinophilic moulds (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton; newer genera Nannizzia, Arthroderma)
- Fungal infections: superficial (pityriasis versicolor, tinea nigra, piedra), cutaneous (dermatophytosis, candidiasis), subcutaneous (mycetoma, sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis), systemic (histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis), opportunistic (aspergillosis, mucormycosis)

**Q2. Classify dermatophytes by habitat.**
- Anthropophilic (human): T. rubrum, T. interdigitale (anthropophilic), T. tonsurans, T. indotineae, E. floccosum — chronic, less inflammatory
- Zoophilic (animals): M. canis, T. mentagrophytes, T. verrucosum — acute, inflammatory
- Geophilic (soil): M. gypseum (Nannizzia gypsea) — inflammatory

**Q3. What is the current dermatophytosis situation in India?**
- Epidemic of chronic, recurrent, extensive and steroid-modified tinea since ~2014
- Main agent now Trichophyton indotineae (ITS genotype VIII of T. mentagrophytes/interdigitale complex) — anthropophilic, spreads within families
- Causes: rampant use of topical steroid–antifungal–antibiotic combinations, incomplete treatment, hot humid climate, tight synthetic clothes, crowding, fomites; terbinafine resistance via squalene epoxidase (SQLE) gene mutations (e.g. Phe397Leu, Leu393Phe)

**Q4. Clinical features of tinea corporis.**
- Annular/arcuate plaques with raised, scaly, active edge (papules, vesicles) and central clearing; itchy; on trunk, limbs
- Variants: tinea imbricata (T. concentricum — concentric rings), bullous, Majocchi's granuloma, kerion-like, tinea profunda, pseudo-imbricata (after steroids)

**Q5. What is tinea incognito (steroid-modified tinea)?**
- Altered appearance after topical/systemic steroids — loss of active edge, less scale, more widespread, pustules, pseudo-imbricata (concentric rings), purpura, striae, bizarre shapes
- KOH often richly positive; mimics eczema, psoriasis, lupus, rosacea (on face)

**Q6. Describe tinea cruris and tinea faciei.**
- Cruris: groin, inner thighs, may spread to buttocks, pubis; scrotum usually spared (unlike candidiasis); men more
- Faciei: non-bearded face, photo-aggravated, often misdiagnosed as lupus or rosacea; may lack scale

**Q7. How do you do a KOH mount and what do you see?**
- Scrape the active edge with a blunt scalpel onto slide, add 10–20% KOH (40% for nails), warm gently, coverslip
- Branched septate hyaline hyphae ± arthroconidia
- Variants: KOH with DMSO, chlorazol black E, Parker ink, calcofluor white (fluorescence) to improve sensitivity

**Q8. Culture media and their uses (Sabouraud's — PYQ).**
- Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) with chloramphenicol and cycloheximide (Mycosel/Mycobiotic) — routine dermatophyte culture at 25–30 °C for up to 4 weeks
- Dermatophyte test medium (DTM) — phenol red turns red with dermatophytes
- Potato dextrose agar (pigment, sporulation), urease test (T. interdigitale positive, T. rubrum negative), hair perforation test, trichophyton agars (vitamin requirements)
- Antifungal susceptibility testing (CLSI M38) and SQLE mutation PCR in resistant cases

**Q9. Differential diagnosis of annular lesions.**
- Nummular eczema, psoriasis, pityriasis rosea (herald patch, collarette), granuloma annulare (no scale), annular lichen planus, erythema annulare centrifugum (trailing scale), subacute cutaneous lupus, Hansen's (BT), seborrhoeic dermatitis, secondary syphilis, sarcoidosis, mycosis fungoides, erythrasma (groin)

**Q10. Topical treatment principles.**
- Apply twice daily to lesion plus 2 cm margin, continue 2 weeks after clinical cure (usually 4–6 weeks)
- Azoles (luliconazole 1%, sertaconazole 2%, eberconazole, clotrimazole, ketoconazole), allylamines (terbinafine 1%, naftifine), amorolfine 0.25%, ciclopirox 1%
- Avoid steroid–antifungal combinations (fixed-dose combination creams)

**Q11. Systemic treatment — Indian consensus.**
- Indications: extensive, multiple sites, recurrent/chronic, failed topical, immunosuppressed
- Itraconazole 100–200 mg/day (5 mg/kg) for 4–8 weeks — currently the most used first-line drug in India; take after a fatty meal, avoid antacids/PPIs
- Terbinafine 250–500 mg/day for 4–6 weeks (higher doses for resistant strains, though failure common with SQLE mutations)
- Griseofulvin, fluconazole (150–300 mg weekly) — less preferred now
- Combination (itraconazole + terbinafine) and voriconazole/posaconazole only for documented refractory cases; continue until clinical and mycological cure

**Q12. What are general measures for recurrence prevention?**
- Treat all family members, wash and sun-dry clothes, iron clothes, loose cotton clothing, don't share towels, keep folds dry, weight loss, stop steroid creams, adherence to full course
- Antifungal powders/soaps as adjuncts; treat tinea pedis/onychomycosis reservoirs

**Q13. What is Majocchi's granuloma?**
- Follicular and dermal invasion by dermatophyte (often T. rubrum) after steroid use or shaving of legs — perifollicular papulopustules/nodules; needs systemic antifungal

**Q14. Why do we see more azole-preferred practice than terbinafine in India today?**
- T. indotineae shows high terbinafine minimum inhibitory concentrations due to SQLE mutations; itraconazole still mostly effective, though rising MIC reports exist

**Q15. Side effects and interactions of itraconazole and terbinafine.**
- Itraconazole: CYP3A4 inhibitor — interactions (statins, warfarin, midazolam, cyclosporine), contraindicated in congestive heart failure (negative inotropy), hepatotoxicity rare, needs acidic stomach
- Terbinafine: taste disturbance, hepatotoxicity (rare), drug rash, SCLE flare, CYP2D6 inhibition (tricyclics, beta-blockers)

**Q16. What is the id reaction (dermatophytid)?**
- Distant sterile eruption (vesicles on palms/fingers, papules) due to hypersensitivity to fungal antigen, usually with inflammatory tinea (kerion, tinea pedis); KOH negative at id site; settles when primary infection is treated

**Q17. Name the specific special forms of tinea.**
- Tinea imbricata (T. concentricum — tribal populations, Pacific/NE India; concentric rings)
- Tinea nigra (Hortaea werneckii — brown macule on palm; not dermatophyte)
- Tinea manuum (one-hand, two-feet syndrome)
- Tinea barbae, tinea capitis, tinea pedis, tinea unguium

## Quick spotter facts
- Active scaly edge + central clearing + KOH hyphae — tinea corporis
- T. indotineae + SQLE mutation = terbinafine-resistant tinea (India)
- Scrotum spared in tinea cruris (involved in candidiasis)

## Note
Doses follow the Indian expert consensus on dermatophytosis (IADVL Task Force); check the department's current protocol.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Superficial fungal infections); Indian expert consensus on dermatophytosis (2018–2023). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
